solution: A \(3 \times 3\) matrix has 9 entries. Each entry can independently be \(-1\) or \(+1\), giving 2 choices per entry. Total number of such matrices \(= 2^9\). Hence (D).

Every orthogonal matrix Q satisfies \(\det(Q) = \pm 1 \neq 0\), so every orthogonal matrix is non-singular. Thus the set of orthogonal matrices is contained in the set of non-singular matrices. There exist non-singular matrices that are not orthogonal, so the containment is proper: Q is a proper subset of P. Hence (B).

Given \(PQ = Q\) and \(QP = P\). Then \(P^2 = P \cdot P = P(QP) = (PQ)P = QP = P\), so \(P^2 = P\). Similarly \(Q^2 = Q \cdot Q = Q(PQ) = (QP)Q = PQ = Q\), so \(Q^2 = Q\). Therefore \(P^2 + Q^2 = P + Q\). Hence (C).

Each corresponding entry of \(A - B\): top-left \(\frac{1}{\pi}[\sin^{-1}(\pi x) - (-\cos^{-1}(\pi x))] = \frac{1}{\pi}[\sin^{-1}(\pi x) + \cos^{-1}(\pi x)] = \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\). The off-diagonal terms \(\tan^{-1}(x/\pi)\) and \(\sin^{-1}(x/\pi)\) cancel to 0. Bottom-right \(\frac{1}{\pi}[\cot^{-1}(\pi x) - (-\tan^{-1}(\pi x))] = \frac{1}{\pi}[\cot^{-1}(\pi x) + \tan^{-1}(\pi x)] = \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\). So \(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1/2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2}I\). Hence (A).

First product: \(\begin{pmatrix} 7 & 1 & 5 \\ 8 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 14+3+5 \\ 16+0+0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 22 \\ 16 \end{pmatrix}\). Add \(5\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\): result \(\begin{pmatrix} 22+5 \\ 16+0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 27 \\ 16 \end{pmatrix}\). Hence (B).

Equating entries: \(2x + y = 1\), \(x + y = 1\), \(p - q = 0\), \(p + q = 0\). From the last two, \(p = 0, q = 0\). Subtracting \(x+y=1\) from \(2x+y=1\) gives \(x = 0\), then \(y = 1\). So \((x, y, p, q) = (0, 1, 0, 0)\). Hence (A).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = 2A\). In general \(A^n = 2^{n-1}A\). For \(n = 2017\), \(A^{2017} = 2^{2016}A\). Hence (B).

Given \(AB = A\) and \(BA = B\). Then \(A^2 = A\cdot A = A(BA) = (AB)A = AA = A^2\); more directly \(A^2 = (AB)A = A(BA) = AB = A\), so A is idempotent. Similarly \(B^2 = (BA)B = B(AB) = BA = B\), so B is idempotent. Both are idempotent. Hence (A).

Let \(M = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ \gamma & -\alpha \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(M^2 = \begin{bmatrix} \alpha^2 + \beta\gamma & 0 \\ 0 & \alpha^2 + \beta\gamma \end{bmatrix} = (\alpha^2 + \beta\gamma)I\). For M to be a square root of the unit matrix, \(M^2 = I\), so \(\alpha^2 + \beta\gamma = 1\), i.e. \(1 - \alpha^2 - \beta\gamma = 0\). Hence (A).

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 9-1 & 3+2 \\ -3-2 & -1+4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). \(5A = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\). So \(A^2 - 5A = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix} = -7I\). Hence (D).

A diagonal matrix of order 4 with \(A^2 = A\) needs each diagonal entry d to satisfy \(d^2 = d\), so \(d \in \{0, 1\}\). There are \(2^4 = 16\) such matrices, but the zero matrix is excluded (we need non-zero). So \(16 - 1 = 15\). Hence (D).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^8 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Setting \(aA + bI = \begin{bmatrix} a+b & 0 \\ a & a+b \end{bmatrix}\), we need \(a = 8\) and \(a + b = 1 \Rightarrow b = -7\). So \((a, b) = (8, -7)\). Hence (C).

RHS: \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3-2 \\ 9-4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}\). LHS: \(-2x + 5y = 1\) and \(3x - y = 5\). From the second, \(y = 3x - 5\); substituting: \(-2x + 5(3x-5) = 1 \Rightarrow 13x = 26 \Rightarrow x = 2, y = 1\). Hence (D).
\((A-B)(A+B) = A^2 + AB - BA - B^2\). This equals \(A^2 - B^2\) if and only if \(AB - BA = 0\), i.e. \(AB = BA\). Hence (C).

P is diagonal with entries \(1, -1, -2\). For each diagonal entry d, \(P^3 + 2P^2\) gives \(d^3 + 2d^2\): for 1, \(1+2 = 3\); for \(-1\), \(-1+2 = 1\); for \(-2\), \(-8+8 = 0\). So \(P^3 + 2P^2 = \mathrm{diag}(3, 1, 0)\). Compare \(2I + P = \mathrm{diag}(3, 1, 0)\). Hence (C).
Check idempotency: row 1 of \(P^2\) first entry \(= 2(2)+(-2)(-1)+(-4)(1) = 4+2-4 = 2\), matching P. Continuing, \(P^2 = P\), so P is idempotent. Therefore \(P^5 = P\). Hence (A).
The scalar e multiplies the matrix: \(e \cdot e^x = e^{x+1} = 1 \Rightarrow x + 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = -1\). Likewise \(e \cdot e^y = 1 \Rightarrow y = -1\). So \((x, y) = (-1, -1)\). Hence (A).

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} x & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} x^2+1 & x \\ x & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Setting \(A^2 = I\): \(x^2 + 1 = 1\) and \(x = 0\), so \(x = 0\). Then \(x^3 + x - 2 = 0 + 0 - 2 = -2\). Hence (B).

For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ a & b & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), the third row of \(A^2\) becomes \([a-a,\ b-b,\ 1] = [0,0,1]\) and the first two rows are unchanged, so \(A^2 = I\). Then \(A^4 = I\), \(A^6 = I\). Thus \(A^2 + 2A^4 + 4A^6 = I + 2I + 4I = 7I\). Since \(A^8 = (A^2)^4 = I\), \(7I = 7A^8\). Hence (A).

\(A\) is a rotation matrix, and \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} \cos n\alpha & \sin n\alpha \\ -\sin n\alpha & \cos n\alpha \end{bmatrix}\). For \(n = 10\), \(A^{10} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos 10\alpha & \sin 10\alpha \\ -\sin 10\alpha & \cos 10\alpha \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (D).

\(A + B\) being defined requires A and B to be of the same order. \(AB\) being defined requires columns of A to equal rows of B. Together with the same order, both A and B must be square matrices of the same order. Hence (C).
\(A^2 = A\) (idempotent), so \(A^3 = A^2 \cdot A = A \cdot A = A^2 = A\). Therefore \((I - A^3) + A = (I - A) + A = I\). Hence (C).

By Cayley-Hamilton, A satisfies its characteristic equation \(\lambda^2 - (\mathrm{tr}A)\lambda + \det A = 0\). Here \(\mathrm{tr}A = 3+1 = 4\), \(\det A = 3-2 = 1\), so \(A^2 - 4A + I = 0\). Comparing with \(A^2 + xA + yI = 0\) gives \(x = -4, y = 1\). Hence (B).
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), repeated multiplication gives \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2n \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (C).

From \(2X + 3Y = O\) and \(X + 2Y = I\): multiply the second by 2 to get \(2X + 4Y = 2I\). Subtract the first: \(Y = 2I\). Then \(X = I - 2Y = I - 4I = -3I = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (C).

Entry (1,1): \(1+\omega+a = 0 \Rightarrow a = -(1+\omega) = \omega^2\) (since \(1+\omega+\omega^2 = 0\)). Entry (2,2): \(-b+2 = 1 \Rightarrow b = 1\). Then \(a^2 + b^2 = (\omega^2)^2 + 1 = \omega^4 + 1 = \omega + 1\) (as \(\omega^4 = \omega\)). So \(a^2 + b^2 = 1 + \omega\). Hence (C).
\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A^2 = 2A\), and in general \(A^n = 2^{n-1}A\). So \(A^{100} = 2^{99}A\). Hence (B).
For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ n & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (C).
\(f(A) = A^2 - 5A\). With \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), from Q500, \(A^2 - 5A = -7I = \begin{bmatrix} -7 & 0 \\ 0 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (A).
Matrix addition is commutative and associative, and matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. The false statement is 'matrix multiplication is commutative'. Hence (C).
\(H = \omega I\) (scalar matrix), so \(H^{70} = \omega^{70}I\). Since \(\omega^3 = 1\), \(\omega^{70} = \omega^{70 \bmod 3} = \omega^1 = \omega\). Thus \(H^{70} = \omega I = H\). Hence (C).

Given \(AB = B\) and \(BA = A\). Then \(A^2 = A \cdot A = A(BA) = (AB)A = BA = A\), so A is idempotent. Also \(B^2 = B \cdot B = B(AB) = (BA)B = AB = B\), so B is idempotent. Both are idempotent. Hence (D).

\(kA = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3k \\ 4k & 5k \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 4a \\ 3b & 60 \end{bmatrix}\). From \(5k = 60\), \(k = 12\). Then \(3k = 4a \Rightarrow 36 = 4a \Rightarrow a = 9\); \(4k = 3b \Rightarrow 48 = 3b \Rightarrow b = 16\). So \((k, a, b) = (12, 9, 16)\). Hence (C).

From \(A + B = 2B'\) substitute \(A = 2B' - B\) into \(3A + 2B = I\): \(3(2B'-B) + 2B = I \Rightarrow 6B' - B = I\). Transposing: \(6B - B' = I\). Adding the two relations: \(5(B + B') = 2I\); subtracting gives \(7(B - B') = 0\), so \(B = B'\). Then \(B + B' = 2B = \frac{2}{5}I \Rightarrow B = \frac{1}{5}I\), and \(A = 2B - B = B = \frac{1}{5}I\). Checking the options: \(10A + 5B = 10(\frac15) + 5(\frac15) = 2 + 1 = 3\), so \(10A + 5B = 3I_3\). Hence (A). [Answer key was blank; derived option A.]

\(A + A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 2\cos 2\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 2\cos 2\theta \end{bmatrix} = 2\cos 2\theta \cdot I\). Setting this equal to I gives \(2\cos 2\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \cos 2\theta = \frac{1}{2} \Rightarrow 2\theta = \frac{\pi}{3} \Rightarrow \theta = \frac{\pi}{6}\). Hence (A).

\(AA^T = 9I\) means rows are mutually orthogonal each with norm 9. Row 3 norm: \(a^2 + 4 + b^2 = 9 \Rightarrow a^2 + b^2 = 5\). Row 1 dot Row 3: \(a + 4 + 2b = 0\). Row 2 dot Row 3: \(2a + 2 - 2b = 0 \Rightarrow a = b - 1\). Substituting into \(a + 2b + 4 = 0\): \((b-1) + 2b + 4 = 0 \Rightarrow 3b + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow b = -1, a = -2\). So \((a, b) = (-2, -1)\). Hence (B).
\((ABA)^T = A^T B^T A^T = ABA\) since \(A = A^T\) and \(B = B^T\). Hence (B).
Given \(P^T = 2P + I\). Transposing: \(P = 2P^T + I = 2(2P + I) + I = 4P + 3I\), so \(-3P = 3I \Rightarrow P = -I\). Then for any nonzero X, \(PX = -IX = -X\). Hence (D).
\([5\ 6\ 2]\) is \(1 \times 3\). The product \([5\ 6\ 2]\cdot A^T = [4\ 8\ 1\ 7\ 8]\) is \(1 \times 5\), so \(A^T\) is \(3 \times 5\). Therefore A is \(5 \times 3\). Hence (D).
If A is both symmetric (\(A = A^T\)) and skew-symmetric (\(A = -A^T\)), then \(A = -A\), so \(2A = 0\), giving \(A = O\), the zero matrix. Hence (B).
For any square matrix A, \((A - A')^T = A^T - A = -(A - A')\), so \(A - A'\) is always skew-symmetric. Hence (D).

The skew-symmetric part is \(B = \frac{1}{2}(M - M^T)\). With \(M = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(M^T = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 3 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(M - M^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Hence (D).

Statement-1: \((ABA)^T = A^T B^T A^T = ABA\) (A, B symmetric), so A(BA) and (AB)A are symmetric — true. Statement-2: \((AB)^T = B^T A^T = BA\), so AB is symmetric iff \(AB = BA\) — true. However ABA is symmetric regardless of whether AB and BA commute, so Statement-2 does not explain Statement-1. Both true but Statement-2 is not a correct explanation. Hence (D).

\((AB)^T = B^T A^T\). For this to equal BA, one sufficient condition is \(A^T = -A\) and \(B^T = -B\) (both skew), giving \(B^T A^T = (-B)(-A) = BA\). Among the options, both A and B skew-symmetric works. Hence (C).
If A is skew-symmetric and n is odd, then \((A^n)^T = (A^T)^n = (-A)^n = (-1)^n A^n = -A^n\). So \(A^n\) is skew-symmetric. Hence (A).

For symmetric A, B: \((A-B)^T\) of \(AB - BA\) gives \((AB-BA)^T = B^T A^T - A^T B^T = BA - AB = -(AB-BA)\), so \(AB - BA\) is skew-symmetric, not symmetric (in general). Thus statement (d) is not true. Hence (D).
For symmetry, the (1,2) and (2,1) entries must be equal: \(x - 1 = 2x + 3 \Rightarrow -4 = x \Rightarrow x = -4\). Hence (C).
\((A + A^T)^T = A^T + A = A + A^T\), so \(A + A^T\) is symmetric. Hence (A).
\(\left[\frac{1}{2}(A - A')\right]^T = \frac{1}{2}(A' - A) = -\frac{1}{2}(A - A')\), so it is skew-symmetric. Hence (B).
\((A + A^T)^T = A^T + A = A + A^T\), so \(A + A^T\) is symmetric. Hence (B).

Given \(A^2 - 5A + 7I = 0\). Statement-I: \(A^2 = 5A - 7I\); multiply by \(A^{-1}\): \(A = 5I - 7A^{-1} \Rightarrow A^{-1} = \frac{1}{7}(5I - A)\) — true. Statement-II: using \(A^2 = 5A - 7I\), \(A^3 = 5A^2 - 7A = 5(5A-7I) - 7A = 18A - 35I\). Then \(A^3 - 2A^2 - 3A + I = (18A-35I) - 2(5A-7I) - 3A + I = 5A - 20I = 5(A - 4I)\) — true. Both statements are true. Hence (A).

\(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{\det A}\,\mathrm{adj}(A)\). \(\det A = 2x\), \(\mathrm{adj}(A) = \begin{bmatrix} x & -1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 & -1/(2x) \\ 0 & 1/x \end{bmatrix}\). Matching the (1,2) entry: \(-\frac{1}{2x} = \frac{1}{6} \Rightarrow 2x = -6 \Rightarrow x = -3\). Hence (A).
\(M = I - X(X'X)^{-1}X'\) is a projection matrix. (i) \(M^2 = M\) (idempotent) — true. (ii) \(MX = X - X(X'X)^{-1}X'X = X - X = O\) — true. Both correct. Hence (C).
\((A+B)(A-B) = A^2 - B^2\) implies \(AB = BA\). Then \(ABA^{-1} = BAA^{-1} = B\), so \((ABA^{-1})^2 = B^2\). Hence (C).
\(A^2 - A + I = O \Rightarrow A^2 = A - I\). Multiply by \(A^{-1}\): \(A = I - A^{-1} \Rightarrow A^{-1} = I - A\). Hence (B).
\(AB = 3I\). Multiply on the left by \(A^{-1}\): \(B = 3A^{-1} \Rightarrow A^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}B\). Hence (B).

With \(2\omega + 1 = z\), \(\omega\) is a non-real cube root of unity, so \(\omega^3 = 1\), \(\omega^7 = \omega\), and \(-\omega^2 - 1 = \omega\). The determinant becomes \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & \omega & \omega^2 \\ 1 & \omega^2 & \omega \end{vmatrix}\). Applying \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\), \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\) and expanding gives \(-3(\omega - \omega^2)\). Since \(\omega - \omega^2 = \sqrt{3}\,i\) and \(z = 2\omega + 1 = \sqrt{3}\,i\), the determinant \(= -3z\). Setting equal to \(3k\): \(k = -z\). Hence (D).
LHS \(= 3 - x^2\). RHS \(= 3(1) - 2(4) = 3 - 8 = -5\). So \(3 - x^2 = -5 \Rightarrow x^2 = 8 \Rightarrow x = \pm 2\sqrt{2}\). Hence (C).

Singular means determinant is zero. \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 4 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Apply \(R_2 \to R_2 - R_1\), \(R_3 \to R_3 - R_1\): \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & a-4 \end{vmatrix} = 1\cdot[(a-4) - 2] = a - 6 = 0 \Rightarrow a = 6\). Hence (D).

Expanding the determinant along Row 1: \(3i(9i \cdot i - (-1)(9)) + 9i(2i - (-1)(10)) + (2\cdot9 - 9i\cdot10)\). The first term \(3i(-9+9) = 0\); the second \(9i(2i+10) = -18 + 90i\); the third \(18 - 90i\). Sum \(= 0 + (-18+90i) + (18-90i) = 0\). So \(x + iy = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0, y = 0\). Hence (D).
The matrix is upper triangular, so \(\det(A) = 4 \cdot k \cdot k = 4k^2 = 256 \Rightarrow k^2 = 64 \Rightarrow |k| = 8\). Hence (D).

The matrix equals \((x-2)I + J\) where J is the all-ones \(3 \times 3\) matrix. Eigenvalues of J are 3, 0, 0, so eigenvalues of the matrix are \((x-2)+3 = x+1\) and \((x-2)+0 = x-2\) (twice). Determinant \(= (x+1)(x-2)^2 = 0\) gives roots \(x = -1\) and \(x = 2\). The distinct roots are \(-1, 2\). Hence (B).
Expanding: \(A = 1(1 + \cos^2\theta) - \cos\theta(-\cos\theta + \cos\theta) + 0 = 1 + \cos^2\theta\). Since \(\cos^2\theta \in [0, 1]\), \(A \in [1, 2]\), the closed interval \([1, 2]\). Hence (A).

This circulant determinant equals \(-(a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc) = -(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca)\). For distinct positive reals, \(a+b+c > 0\) and \(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca > 0\), so the determinant is negative, i.e. \(< 0\). Hence (A).

Expanding gives \(xyz\left(1 + \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right) = 0\). Since \(x, y, z \neq 0\), \(xyz \neq 0\), so \(1 + x^{-1} + y^{-1} + z^{-1} = 0 \Rightarrow x^{-1} + y^{-1} + z^{-1} = -1\). Hence (D).

Replace \(R_2\) by \(R_2 - R_1 - R_3\), which gives \([-4, 0, 0]\). Expanding along this row: \(\det = 4[(x+1)(2x-1) - (x-2)(2x-1)] = 4(2x-1)[(x+1)-(x-2)] = 4(2x-1)(3) = 12(2x-1) = 24x - 12\). Comparing with \(ax - 12\) gives \(a = 24\). Hence (B).

M is symmetric, so \(M + M^T = 2M\), and \(3(M + M^T) = 6M = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 6 & 0 \\ 6 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). Its determinant \(= -6^3 = -216\). Then \(\frac{1}{3}(-216) = -72\). Hence (C).

Here \(\alpha, \beta\) are the non-real cube roots of unity, so \(\alpha + \beta = -1\), \(\alpha\beta = 1\), \(\alpha^2 = \beta\), \(\beta^2 = \alpha\), and \(\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = -1\). Expanding the determinant: the diagonal product gives \((\lambda+1)(\lambda^2 - \lambda) - \alpha^2\lambda - \beta^2\lambda = \lambda(\lambda^2-1) - \lambda(\alpha^2+\beta^2) = \lambda^3 - \lambda - \lambda(-1) = \lambda^3\). Hence (B).

Since \(\sin 75^\circ = \cos 15^\circ\) and \(\cos 75^\circ = \sin 15^\circ\), the determinant \(= \cos 15^\circ\cos 75^\circ - \sin 15^\circ\sin 75^\circ = \cos 15^\circ\sin 15^\circ - \sin 15^\circ\cos 15^\circ = 0\). Hence (A).
\(P = x^2 - 1\). \(Q = \begin{vmatrix} x & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & x \end{vmatrix} = x^3 - 3x + 2\). Then \(\frac{dQ}{dx} = 3x^2 - 3 = 3(x^2 - 1) = 3P\). Hence (B).

For \(x^3 + a^2 x + b = 0\) the coefficient of \(x^2\) is 0, so \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0\). The circulant determinant equals \(-(\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 - 3\alpha\beta\gamma)\). Since \(\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 0\), \(\alpha^3 + \beta^3 + \gamma^3 = 3\alpha\beta\gamma\), so the bracket is zero and the determinant is 0. Hence (D).

This is a circulant determinant with first row \((c_0, c_1, c_2) = (a^2, 2ab, b^2)\), equal to \(c_0^3 + c_1^3 + c_2^3 - 3c_0c_1c_2 = a^6 + 8a^3b^3 + b^6 - 6a^3b^3 = a^6 + 2a^3b^3 + b^6 = (a^3 + b^3)^2\). Hence (B).
\(|A| = 1\cdot 1 - (\log_b a)(\log_a b) = 1 - 1 = 0\), since \(\log_b a \cdot \log_a b = 1\). Hence (A).
For a \(3 \times 3\) determinant with entries 0 or 1, the maximum value is 2 (achieved e.g. by an appropriate 0-1 matrix). Hence (B).

\(f(x) = \begin{vmatrix} x & \lambda \\ 2\lambda & x \end{vmatrix} = x^2 - 2\lambda^2\). \(f(\lambda x) = (\lambda x)^2 - 2\lambda^2 = \lambda^2 x^2 - 2\lambda^2\). So \(f(\lambda x) - f(x) = \lambda^2 x^2 - 2\lambda^2 - (x^2 - 2\lambda^2) = x^2(\lambda^2 - 1)\). Hence (D).
\(\det(A) = a^2 - xy = a^2 - 1\) (since \(xy = 1\)). Then \(\det(AA^T) = \det(A)\det(A^T) = (\det A)^2 = (a^2 - 1)^2\). Hence (D).
\(\det(A) = (\log x)(2) - (-1)(-\log x) = 2\log x - \log x = \log x = 2\). With natural log, \(x = e^2\). Hence (B).

Expanding, \(f(x) = a^3 + 2a^2 x + a x^2\). Then \(f(2x) - f(x) = (a^3 + 4a^2x + 4ax^2) - (a^3 + 2a^2x + ax^2) = 2a^2x + 3ax^2 = ax(2a + 3x)\). This is divisible by x, by a, and by \(2a + 3x\) — i.e. by all of options (a), (b), (c). So it is not divisible by none of these. Hence (D).
A determinant is a single number (scalar) associated to a square matrix. Hence (C).
The matrix is Hermitian (each \(a_{ij}\) is the complex conjugate of \(a_{ji}\), diagonal entries real). The determinant of a Hermitian matrix is real, so z is purely real. Hence (A).

A is upper triangular, so \(\det(A) = 5 \cdot \alpha \cdot 5 = 25\alpha\). Then \(|A^2| = |A|^2 = (25\alpha)^2 = 625\alpha^2 = 25 \Rightarrow \alpha^2 = \frac{1}{25} \Rightarrow |\alpha| = \frac{1}{5}\). Hence (A).
Expanding the determinant and taking its Maclaurin expansion gives \(f(x) = 1 - 2x + \frac{5}{2}x^2 + \cdots\). The coefficient of x is \(-2\). Hence (B).

\(A(\text{adj} A) = |A| I\). With \(|A| = 2\) (order 2), \(A(\text{adj} A) = 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\). Matches option B.
\(A(\text{adj} A) = |A| I\). Given \(= 5I\) for order 3, so \(|A| = 5\). Then \(|\text{adj} A| = |A|^{n-1} = |A|^2 = 25\). Matches option B.

For an order-3 matrix, each application of adj raises the determinant to the power \((n-1) = 2\). Applying adj three times: \(\det(\text{adj}(\text{adj}(\text{adj} A))) = |A|^{2^3} = |A|^8 = 3^8 = 6561 = 81^2\). Matches option A.
\(|(2A)^{-1}| = \dfrac{1}{|2A|} = \dfrac{1}{2^3 |A|} = \dfrac{1}{8 \times 3} = \dfrac{1}{24}\). Matches option C.

For invertible \(A, B\): \((AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}\) (reversal law), which always holds. The other options (\(AB = BA\), \((A+B)(A-B) = A^2 - B^2\)) fail since matrices need not commute. Matches option C.
For order 3, \(\text{adj}(\text{adj} A) = |A|^{n-2} A = |A|^{1} A = |A| A\). Matches option D.
\(\det(B^{-1}AB) = \det(B^{-1})\det(A)\det(B) = \dfrac{1}{\det B}\det(A)\det(B) = \det(A)\). Matches option C.

For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix: \(\text{adj}(\text{adj} A) = |A|^{n-2}A = |A|^0 A = A\) — Statement-1 is TRUE. And \(|\text{adj} A| = |A|^{n-1} = |A|^1 = |A|\) — Statement-2 is TRUE. However, Statement-1 follows from \(n - 2 = 0\) directly, not from Statement-2; the determinant identity in Statement-2 is a separate consequence and does not by itself explain \(\text{adj}(\text{adj} A) = A\). So both true, but Statement-2 is not a correct explanation. Matches option A.

\(A\) is a rotation matrix, which is orthogonal: \(A^T A = I\), hence \(A^T = A^{-1}\). (Note \(A^T = A\) only if \(\sin\theta = 0\), and \(A^2 = I\) only for special \(\theta\); neither holds for general \(0 < \theta < \pi\).) Matches option D.
The matrix is upper-triangular, so \(\det = \lambda \cdot 2 \cdot \lambda = 2\lambda^2\). It is non-singular iff \(\det \ne 0\) iff \(\lambda \ne 0\). Matches option C.
\(\det(B^{-1}AB) = \det(B^{-1})\det(A)\det(B) = \det(A)\) (the \(B\) factors cancel). Matches option D.
From \(AB = AC\), if \(A\) is non-singular (invertible), left-multiplying by \(A^{-1}\) gives \(B = C\). If \(A\) is singular, cancellation may fail. Matches option B.

If \(A\) has integer entries and \(\det A = \pm 1\), then \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det A}\text{adj} A = \pm \text{adj} A\). The adjoint of an integer matrix has integer entries (cofactors are sums/products of integers). So \(A^{-1}\) exists and all its entries are integers. Matches option D.
A skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has determinant 0 (since \(\det A = \det(-A^T) = (-1)^n \det A = -\det A\) for odd \(n\)). A singular matrix has no inverse. Matches option D.
\(|\text{adj} A| = |A|^{n-1} = |A|^{3-1} = 8^2\). Matches option B.

\(AB = I\) means \(B = A^{-1}\). For \(A(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & \tan\theta \\ -\tan\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), \(\det A = 1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta\), and \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\sec^2\theta}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tan\theta \\ \tan\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Thus \((\sec^2\theta)B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -\tan\theta \\ \tan\theta & 1 \end{pmatrix} = A(-\theta)\). Matches option C.

A homogeneous system has infinitely many (non-trivial) solutions iff the coefficient determinant is zero: \(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 4 & -\lambda \\ 4 & \lambda & 2 \\ \lambda & 2 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), which gives \(\lambda^3 + 4\lambda - 40 = 0\). This cubic has exactly one real root (its discriminant is negative for the other two). So the number of real values of \(\lambda\) is 1. Matches option B.

Three equations in two unknowns are consistent iff \(\begin{vmatrix} \lambda & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -3 & -\lambda \\ 3 & -2 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(-2\lambda^2 + 6\lambda + 8 = 0\), i.e. \(\lambda^2 - 3\lambda - 4 = 0\), so \(\lambda = -1\) or \(\lambda = 4\). Matches option D.

The coefficient determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 8 & -3 & -5 \\ 5 & -8 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 \end{vmatrix} = 0\) (each row sums to zero). A homogeneous system with zero determinant has infinitely many non-zero solutions. Matches option D.

Non-trivial solution requires \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & \lambda & -1 \\ \lambda & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & -\lambda \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(\lambda^3 - \lambda = 0\), so \(\lambda = 0, 1, -1\) — exactly three values. Matches option D.

The third equation \(2x + 8y - 6z = 7\) has coefficients exactly twice those of the first (\(x + 4y - 3z\)), but \(2 \times 3 = 6 \ne 7\). So the system is inconsistent (rank of coefficient matrix \(= 2 <\) rank of augmented matrix \(= 3\)): no solutions. Matches option C.

Equations 2 and 3 both contain \(x + 2y\). For no solution, the coefficient determinant must be zero AND the system inconsistent. The determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & a \end{vmatrix} = a - 3 = 0\) gives \(a = 3\). Then equation 3 becomes \(x + 2y + 3z = b\), but equation 2 is \(x + 2y + 3z = 10\); these are inconsistent unless \(b = 10\). So no solution when \(a = 3\), \(b \ne 10\). Matches option A.

A unique solution exists iff the coefficient determinant is non-zero. The determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 5 & -1 & \alpha \\ 2 & 3 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = 23 - \alpha\) depends only on \(\alpha\), not on \(\beta\). So existence of a unique solution depends on \(\alpha\) only. Matches option A.
Unique solution iff coefficient determinant \(\ne 0\): \(\begin{vmatrix} 3 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & a \end{vmatrix} = 2 - a\). This is non-zero iff \(a \ne 2\). Matches option D.

Non-zero solution of a homogeneous system requires the coefficient determinant to be zero: \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & k & -1 \\ 3 & -k & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 6 - 6k = 0\), so \(k = 1\). Matches option C.

No solution requires \(\det = 0\) and inconsistency. \(\det = (k+1)(k+3) - 8k = k^2 - 4k + 3 = 0\) gives \(k = 1\) or \(k = 3\). At \(k = 1\) the system is consistent (infinite solutions); at \(k = 3\) it is inconsistent (no solution). So exactly 1 value (\(k = 3\)) gives no solution. Matches option A.

MULTI-KEY (B and C). This homogeneous system has coefficient determinant equal to the Vandermonde determinant \((\beta - \alpha)(\gamma - \alpha)(\gamma - \beta)\). If \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are distinct, the determinant is non-zero, so the only solution is the trivial one (a unique solution) — statement C correct. If any two of \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) are equal, the determinant is zero, giving infinitely many solutions — statement B correct. (Option a is wrong since it isn't unique when two are equal; option d is wrong since a homogeneous system never has a finite number \(> 1\) of solutions.)

Non-trivial solution requires the coefficient determinant to be zero: \(\begin{vmatrix} t & t+1 & t-1 \\ t+1 & t & t+2 \\ t-1 & t+2 & t \end{vmatrix} = -8t - 4 = 0\), giving \(t = -1/2\) — exactly one real value. Matches option C.

Writing the system as \((A - \alpha I)\mathbf{x} = 0\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), infinite solutions occur when \(\alpha\) is an eigenvalue. The characteristic polynomial \(-\alpha^3 + 3\alpha^2 + 42\alpha + 108 = 0\) has one real root (\(\alpha = 9\)) and a complex conjugate pair. So the number of real \(\alpha\) is 1. Matches option A.

Coefficient determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} \lambda & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \lambda + 1\). For \(\lambda \ne -1\) the determinant is non-zero, giving a unique solution (so options a and c are wrong). For \(\lambda = -1\): equation 1 becomes \(-x + y + z = 3\) and equation 3 is \(-x + y + z = \mu\); these are consistent (infinite solutions) iff \(\mu = 3\). Matches option B.

The coefficient matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & p+2 \\ 0 & 2p+1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) has determinant \(-(2p^2 + 5p + 2) = -(2p+1)(p+2)\), zero at \(p = -2\) and \(p = -1/2\). Checking consistency: at \(p = -1/2\) the system has a solution (infinite); at \(p = -2\) the system is inconsistent (equation 2 becomes \(0 = 3\)). So no solution when \(p = -2\). Matches option B.

The coefficient determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & -1 \\ 3 & 5 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 10 \ne 0\). A homogeneous system with non-zero determinant has only the trivial solution \(x = y = z = 0\). Matches option B.

Unique solution iff coefficient determinant \(\ne 0\): \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & \lambda \end{vmatrix} = \lambda - 3\). This is non-zero iff \(\lambda \ne 3\), in which case \(\mu\) may be any value. Matches option D.

Three equations in two unknowns are consistent iff \(\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 & -5 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -14 & -a \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(5a + 80 = 0\), so \(a = -16\), which is none of the listed values 1, 2, 5. Matches option D (None of these).

The coefficient determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 0\) (row 3 = row 1 + row 2). But the augmented system has rank 3 (the constants 3, 3, 1 do not satisfy \(b_3 = b_1 + b_2\), since \(3 + 3 = 6 \ne 1\)). So rank(coeff) \(= 2 <\) rank(aug) \(= 3\): no solution. Matches option D.

Non-trivial solution requires the coefficient determinant zero: \(\begin{vmatrix} a & a & -1 \\ b & -1 & b \\ -1 & c & c \end{vmatrix} = 0\), giving \(-2abc - ab - ac - bc + 1 = 0\), i.e. \(2abc + ab + bc + ca = 1\). Adding \(1 + a + b + c + (ab+bc+ca) + abc = (1+a)(1+b)(1+c)\), one finds \(\dfrac{1}{1+a} + \dfrac{1}{1+b} + \dfrac{1}{1+c} = 2\) (verified numerically for any \(a, b, c\) satisfying the determinant condition). Matches option C.
Non-trivial solution requires \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4a & a \\ 1 & 3b & b \\ 1 & 2c & c \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(ab - 2ac + bc = 0\), so \(ab + bc = 2ac\). Matches option A.
Non-trivial solution requires \(\begin{vmatrix} 2k & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & k & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & k \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(2k^3 - 4k - 8 = 0\), whose only real root is \(k = 2\). Matches option A.
Non-trivial solution requires \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & k & 3 \\ 3 & k & -2 \\ 2 & 3 & -4 \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(33 - 2k = 0\), so \(k = 33/2\). Matches option A.

The coefficient determinant \(\begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\), but the augmented matrix has rank 3 (rank coeff \(= 2\)). So the system is inconsistent: it has 0 solutions. Matches option D.
Non-zero solution of the homogeneous system requires \(\begin{vmatrix} a & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & a & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = 0\). This factors as \((a-1)^2 = 0\), so \(a = 1\). Matches option C.

The coefficient matrix is upper-triangular: \(\begin{pmatrix} K & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & K-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & K+2 \end{pmatrix}\) with determinant \(K(K-1)(K+2)\). A unique solution requires the determinant \(\ne 0\), i.e. \(K \notin \{0, 1, -2\}\). Among the options, only \(K = -1\) gives a non-zero determinant. Matches option B.

Non-zero solution requires \(\begin{vmatrix} a & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & a & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & a \end{vmatrix} = 0\). Expanding gives \(a^3 + 3a = a(a^2 + 3) = 0\). The only real root is \(a = 0\). Matches option D.
